items.stimulus: In 1994, the city of Riverton began restoring a marsh along Harbor Creek. For decades, engineers had straightened the creek and drained parts of the marsh to make room for roads and buildings. Ecologist Lena Ortiz directed the project's initial survey. Her team mapped tidal pools, measured salinity, and recorded the fish and bird species that used the area. These measurements showed that the remaining wetlands provided habitat for juvenile fish and absorbed storm water. <u>Because Harbor Creek connects to the bay, the marsh also receives fresh water with each high tide.</u> Using the survey results, the city removed several concrete barriers that had blocked the creek's natural flow. Workers replanted cordgrass and other native marsh plants along the exposed banks. Volunteers returned each spring to count plant stems and photograph the pools from fixed locations. The restored marsh lies two blocks from Riverton's public baseball stadium. <u>The stadium's scoreboard was replaced in 2001 with a larger electronic display.</u> By 2010, the marsh absorbed more storm water and supported more species than it had before the project. Today, Harbor Creek Marsh demonstrates how careful research can guide the restoration of an urban ecosystem.
items.explanation: The scoreboard detail does not advance the passage's focus on researching and restoring the marsh. It should be deleted because it wanders to an unrelated subject.
